title: Weeping and shouting (Ezra 3:10–13)
hook: the temple foundation is laid; the young shout, the old weep, and no one can tell the sounds apart

segments.voice: Yesterday, Esther and the feast of Purim, and your line was for such a time as this.

Two days ago the temple burned. Today, in the story, the people are back. The book of Ezra opens with a Persian king, Cyrus, giving the exiles leave to go home to Jerusalem and build the house of the Lord again. Some go. They set up the altar first, on its old bases, and then, with stonecutters, carpenters and cedar wood brought by sea, they start on the foundation. On the day it's laid, the priests stand in their robes with trumpets, the Levites with cymbals, and they sing together by turns. Then the writer reaches for a strange sentence.

The song is short. They praise the Lord "because he is good, for his mercy endureth for ever toward Israel," and the people shout with a great shout. But not everyone shouts. "Many of the priests and Levites and chief of the fathers, who were ancient men, that had seen the first house, when the foundation of this house was laid before their eyes, wept with a loud voice." The old ones remember. What they see now is a beginning, and maybe a smaller one. So they weep, loudly, while many others shout for joy. Then the strange sentence: "So that the people could not discern the noise of the shout of joy from the noise of the weeping of the people: for the people shouted with a loud shout, and the noise was heard afar off." From far enough away, you'd hear one sound. The writer doesn't correct either group. Nobody tells the old men to cheer up, and nobody tells the young ones to hush out of respect. Both sounds belong to the day. Something precious was lost, something real is beginning, and the text lets both rise together. Some readers think of this scene at weddings after a death in the family, at a new church building where the old one stood, at a graduation a grandparent didn't live to see. One sound, heard afar off.

Bring to mind something in your life that's mixed: a move, a new job, a child leaving home, a recovery, a change that's good and still costs something. Let the joy come up, and when the grief comes too, let them sit side by side without deciding which one wins. If you pray, bring both to God together; if you don't, let your breath carry both.
Cyrus. The Persian king who let the exiles go home, where the old wept and the young shouted for joy as the new temple's foundation was laid.
Your line: joy and grief, one sound. Neither one has to wait its turn. Day seven hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Christians sometimes read Ezra 3 at the dedication of a new church building or at moments of new beginning after loss, and some churches mark such days with both thanksgiving and remembrance.

fork.setup: you're one of the old men. you remember the first temple. now you stand at a new foundation while the crowd shouts for joy. what do you do?
options: stay home rather than spoil the day.
fork.reveal: they wept with a loud voice, right there in the crowd, and the text lets their weeping and the shouting rise as one sound.

chat.says: At the new temple's foundation, why were some people crying while others cheered?
options: The old ones remembered the first temple; the joy and the grief were both true.
They cried because the king had refused to let them finish building.
The crying was a mistake, and the leaders told them to cheer up.
chat.meaning: The old men who had seen the first house wept aloud while others shouted, and the text corrects neither. Both sounds belonged to the day.

Cyrus.meaning: the Persian king who let the exiles go home

Levites.meaning: temple helpers who stood with cymbals and sang

Ezra.meaning: the book that tells of the exiles' return
